interviewQuestions.question: How do you prepare for a remote pair-programming interview beyond studying the technical material?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat the mechanics as fully within my control and prepare for them the day before, not the morning of. That means installing and actually testing whatever tool the invite names — a Live Share extension, a specific shared-repl link — rather than assuming a similar tool I already know will behave the same way. I also check my connection is stable, ideally wired, and set my editor's font size up for screen-share legibility ahead of time.

For example, before a round that specified VS Code Live Share, I installed it and did a five-minute test session with a friend the night before, which caught that my firewall was blocking the connection — something I'd rather discover then than during the scored round itself.

If the invite doesn't specify a tool, I ask the recruiter beforehand. It's a low-risk, completely normal question that removes a real source of avoidable friction.

**Testing:** whether you take ownership of the parts of the interview you fully control, rather than treating tooling friction as bad luck.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Preparing for the mechanics

interviewQuestions.question: What's your approach to narrating your actions during a live remote pairing session?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I narrate intent before I act, not syntax as I type — "I'm going to check how this function is tested before changing it" rather than reading my code aloud character by character, which adds noise without adding understanding. The reasoning is that a remote partner can't see my face or infer what I'm about to do the way an in-person pair would, so verbal narration is the only substitute channel they have.

I've found this matters even for small, obviously-correct changes — silently fixing something, even correctly, leaves the interviewer watching a cursor move with no context, which undercuts the exact collaboration signal the round exists to test. A two-second heads-up before a rename or a quick fix keeps my partner oriented the whole time.

I also try to narrate at decision points more than at mechanical ones — explaining why I'm choosing one approach over another matters more than narrating every keystroke.

**Testing:** whether you understand that in a remote format, narration isn't optional politeness — it's the primary channel carrying the collaboration signal being evaluated.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Narration discipline

interviewQuestions.question: What would you do if the collaboration tool broke or your connection dropped in the middle of a pairing interview?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd say so immediately rather than silently struggling — "this isn't reconnecting, want to try refreshing, or should we switch to you sharing your screen instead?" Proposing a concrete fallback shows composure on a problem that's clearly not my fault, and most interviewers have a fallback ready since this isn't a rare occurrence.

On reconnecting, I'd briefly restate what I was doing right before the drop — "I was mid-way through adding validation to the create endpoint" — so we pick back up with shared context instead of losing several minutes to re-explaining. I try not to over-apologize; a brief acknowledgment and moving forward reads better than dwelling on something outside my control.

I also keep a backup communication channel in mind before the round starts — a phone number or a secondary video link — in case the primary tool goes down entirely rather than just lagging.

**Testing:** whether you stay composed and solution-oriented through an unplanned technical failure, since a reasonable evaluator discounts for the failure itself and evaluates your reaction to it instead.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Handling a technical failure mid-session

interviewQuestions.question: Beyond writing correct code, what does it mean to take ownership of a remote pairing session?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I think of it as light ownership of the session itself, not just the code inside it — confirming at the start that the tool actually works both ways ("can you see my cursor and hear me clearly?"), noticing early if the pace feels off and naming it rather than letting time quietly slip, and keeping a rough mental time budget without needing the interviewer to manage it for me.

On a real remote team, this is exactly the instinct that keeps a pairing session or a meeting productive — it's a shared responsibility everyone in the room takes on instinctively, not solely the facilitator's job. I've found interviewers who've worked remotely for years notice candidates who already carry this habit into the interview itself.

Concretely, in a round where I sensed we were behind schedule around the halfway mark, I said so directly and proposed cutting a planned sub-task rather than letting us run out of time implicitly — that kind of proactive session management is itself a positive signal, separate from the code produced.

**Testing:** whether you extend ownership beyond your own code to the shared process, which is a distinctly senior-level habit in distributed teams.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Owning the session, not just the code
